body:
There seems to be some inconsistency in how the engine tries to prevent you from calling `free()` on the underlying object from within a script.

| | Debug | Release |
|-|-|-|
| calling `free()` directly | Works (`is_instance_valid(self)` returns `false` afterwards) | Script doesn't compile |
| `call("free")` | Breaks with "Object is locked and can't be freed." | Works sometimes, crashes sometimes |

It's probably alright for the Release build to crash, but it's not ideal that the Debug build makes it look like this works (possible simply due to the debug heap clearing freed memory). Since the Release build is able to catch this issue during script compilation, maybe this check can somehow be brought to Debug builds, too.

Is it incorrect to call free() on self? I have always used queue_free(), but decided to try using free() this time for a new project and ran into this issue. If so, should free() should only be called on other scripts or nodes? I want to be sure I am doing it correctly. Thank you for the help.

Long story short: Yes, `queue_free()` is definitely the way to go here. This causes the engine to delete the node (and possibly the script) at a later point in the frame when all `_process()` and `_physics_process()` functions have completed, so there's no race condition about possibly still executing code within the script at that point. It's okay to remove the node from the scene tree at the same time, so it's gone immediately in terms of the scene hierarchy, but it's not gone for anyone in the middle of doing something with it.

Long story long: Whether it's okay for executing code to delete "itself" (or rather an object representing it), is handled differently in different contexts. In C++, for example, it's not uncommon to call `delete this`, because the executable code exists independently of the current object instance. If, on the other hand, code inside a DLL would call `FreeLibrary()` on its own DLL, this would probably crash, because the DLL including the code contained therein may be removed from memory while that code is still executing.

For Godot, the script is typically a resource of the node it's attached to, so if that node is freed and no other node is currently using the same script, the engine will probably destroy the script resource along with the node. If this is triggered from within the running script, it's a bit of a gamble what happens when the engine continues to execute what are now random values in memory, but a crash is certainly a likely outcome.

It looks like there are some safeguards like `call("free")` having an explicit debug-mode check for this scenario and the script compiler not even recognizing a "free" member on the "self" object. That's not entirely foolproof, though. You can sneakily work around it by doing
```gdscript
var myself = self
myself.free()
```
It will then happily free "myself" in a Release build. And crash.
